claim: Calsyntenins are atypical cadherins encoded by three genes in mammals (Clstn1-3 in mice) and a single gene in Drosophila, C. elegans, and other invertebrates.
source: Calsyntenins (a.k.a. alcadeins) are atypical cadherins that are encoded by three genes in mammals (Clstn1-3 in mice) and a single gene in Drosophila, C. elegans, and other invertebrates (Araki et al., 2003; Hintsch et al., 2002; Ohno et al., 2014; Vogt et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature (Araki et al., 2003; Hintsch et al., 2002; Ohno et al., 2014; Vogt et al., 2001).

claim: Calsyntenins are type I membrane proteins containing two N-terminal cadherin domains followed by a single LNS-domain, a transmembrane region, and a short cytoplasmic tail.
source: Calsyntenins are type I membrane proteins containing two N-terminal cadherin domains followed by a single LNS-domain (also referred to as LG-domain), a transmembrane region, and a short cytoplasmic tail.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about calsyntenins presented as a factual statement.

claim: Calsyntenins are primarily expressed in neurons.
source: Calsyntenins are primarily expressed in neurons, although a variant of Clstn3 with a different non-cadherin extracellular sequence is present in adipocytes (referred to as Clstn3β; Zeng et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation (Zeng et al., 2019) and represents established knowledge about calsyntenin expression patterns.

claim: A variant of Clstn3 with a different non-cadherin extracellular sequence is present in adipocytes.
source: Calsyntenins are primarily expressed in neurons, although a variant of Clstn3 with a different non-cadherin extracellular sequence is present in adipocytes (referred to as Clstn3β; Zeng et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Zeng et al., 2019.

claim: All calsyntenins were localized by immunoelectron microscopy to postsynaptic densities of excitatory synapses in cortex and cerebellum.
source: The first view positing a role for calsyntenins as postsynaptic adhesion molecules was spawned by the localization of all calsyntenins by immunoelectron microscopy to postsynaptic densities of excitatory synapses in cortex and cerebellum (Hintsch et al., 2002; Vogt et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Hintsch et al., 2002; Vogt et al., 2001).

claim: Calsyntenins induce presynaptic specializations in heterologous synapse formation assays when expressed in non-neuronal cells.
source: In further support of this view, calsyntenins were shown to induce presynaptic specializations in heterologous synapse formation assays when expressed in non-neuronal cells (Pettem et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Pettem et al., 2013.

claim: Clstn3 KO mice display a 20–30% decrease in excitatory synapse density in the CA1 region of the hippocampus.
source: Careful analyses revealed that Clstn3 KO mice display a 20–30% decrease in excitatory synapse density in the CA1 region of the hippocampus (Kim et al., 2020; Pettem et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Kim et al., 2020; Pettem et al., 2013).

claim: Pettem et al., 2013 observed a similar decrease in inhibitory synapse density in the CA1 region.
source: In addition, Pettem et al., 2013 observed a similar decrease in inhibitory synapse density in the CA1 region, although Kim et al., 2020 failed to detect such a decrease.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Pettem et al., 2013.

claim: Kim et al., 2020 failed to detect a decrease in inhibitory synapse density in the CA1 region.
source: In addition, Pettem et al., 2013 observed a similar decrease in inhibitory synapse density in the CA1 region, although Kim et al., 2020 failed to detect such a decrease.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kim et al., 2020.

claim: Pettem et al., 2013 reported a 30–40% decrease in mEPSC and mIPSC frequency in Clstn3 KO mice.
source: Moreover, Pettem et al., 2013 reported a 30–40% decrease in mEPSC and mIPSC frequency, but unexpectedly found no change in excitatory synaptic strength as measured by input/output curves.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Pettem et al., 2013.

claim: Pettem et al., 2013 found no change in excitatory synaptic strength as measured by input/output curves in Clstn3 KO mice.
source: Moreover, Pettem et al., 2013 reported a 30–40% decrease in mEPSC and mIPSC frequency, but unexpectedly found no change in excitatory synaptic strength as measured by input/output curves.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Pettem et al., 2013.

claim: The Clstn2 KO decreased the inhibitory synapse density in the hippocampus by approximately 10–20%.
source: Similar analyses showed that the Clstn2 KO also decreased the inhibitory synapse density in the hippocampus by approximately 10–20% (Lipina et al., 2016), whereas the Clstn1 KO modestly impaired excitatory synapses in juvenile but not in adult mice (Ster et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lipina et al., 2016.

claim: The Clstn1 KO modestly impaired excitatory synapses in juvenile but not in adult mice.
source: Similar analyses showed that the Clstn2 KO also decreased the inhibitory synapse density in the hippocampus by approximately 10–20% (Lipina et al., 2016), whereas the Clstn1 KO modestly impaired excitatory synapses in juvenile but not in adult mice (Ster et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ster et al., 2014.

claim: Pettem et al., 2013 and Lu et al., 2014 showed that the LNS domain of calsyntenins binds to an N-terminal sequence of α-neurexins that is not shared by β-neurexins.
source: Pettem et al., 2013 and (Lu et al., 2014) showed that the LNS domain of calsyntenins binds to an N-terminal sequence ofα-neurexins that is not shared by β-neurexins.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pettem et al., 2013 and Lu et al., 2014.

claim: Kim et al., 2020 demonstrated that the cadherin domains of calsyntenins bind to the 6th LNS domain of neurexins that is shared by α- and β-neurexins.
source: Kim et al., 2020, in contrast, demonstrated that the cadherin domains of calsyntenins bind to the 6th LNS domain of neurexins that is shared by α- and β-neurexins.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kim et al., 2020.

claim: Um et al., 2014 did not detect any direct binding of calsyntenins to neurexins.
source: Adding to this puzzle, Um et al., 2014 did not detect any direct binding of calsyntenins to neurexins, and no study has reconstituted a stable calsyntenin-neurexin complex.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Um et al., 2014.

claim: No study has reconstituted a stable calsyntenin-neurexin complex.
source: Adding to this puzzle, Um et al., 2014 did not detect any direct binding of calsyntenins to neurexins, and no study has reconstituted a stable calsyntenin-neurexin complex.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the state of the literature, representing an inference from the absence of published evidence.

claim: Calsyntenins localize to transport vesicles containing APP.
source: This view was motivated by the localization of calsyntenins to transport vesicles containing APP (Araki et al., 2007; Konecna et al., 2006; Vagnoni et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Araki et al., 2007; Konecna et al., 2006; Vagnoni et al., 2012).

claim: A cytoplasmic sequence of calsyntenins binds to kinesins.
source: A cytoplasmic sequence of calsyntenins binds to kinesins (Konecna et al., 2006), and at least Clstn1 found in vesicles containing kinesin (Ludwig et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Konecna et al., 2006.

claim: Clstn1 is found in vesicles containing kinesin.
source: A cytoplasmic sequence of calsyntenins binds to kinesins (Konecna et al., 2006), and at least Clstn1 found in vesicles containing kinesin (Ludwig et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ludwig et al., 2009.

claim: Calsyntenins are present in a molecular complex with presynaptic GABAB-receptors and APP.
source: Moreover, carefully controlled immunoprecipitations showed that calsyntenins are present in a molecular complex with presynaptic GABAB-receptors and APP (Dinamarca et al., 2019; Schwenk et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Dinamarca et al., 2019; Schwenk et al., 2016).

claim: Clstn1 KO mice exhibited only modest changes in APP transport and in the proteolytic processing of APP into Aβ peptides.
source: However, Clstn1 KO mice exhibited only modest changes in APP transport and in the proteolytic processing of APP into Aβ peptides, and Clstn2 KO mice displayed no changes in these parameters (Gotoh et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gotoh et al., 2020.

claim: Clstn2 KO mice displayed no changes in APP transport and proteolytic processing.
source: However, Clstn1 KO mice exhibited only modest changes in APP transport and in the proteolytic processing of APP into Aβ peptides, and Clstn2 KO mice displayed no changes in these parameters (Gotoh et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gotoh et al., 2020.

claim: The Clstn1 KO simultaneously increased the levels of the C-terminal cleavage fragment (CTF) of APP and of Aβ peptides without changing APP levels.
source: Furthermore, the Clstn1 KO simultaneously increased the levels of the C-terminal cleavage fragment (CTF) of APP and of Aβ peptides without changing APP levels, making it difficult to understand how a decreased APP cleavage causing increased CTF levels could also elevate Aβ levels (Gotoh et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gotoh et al., 2020.

claim: All three calsyntenins are expressed in the CA1 and CA3 regions and the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus.
source: We confirmed that all three calsyntenins were expressed in the CA1 and CA3 regions and the dentate gyrus (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from single-molecule in situ hybridization shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In the CA1 region, Clstn1 and Clstn3 levels were highest.
source: In the CA1 region, Clstn1 and Clstn3 levels were highest; in the CA3 region, all three calsyntenins were similarly abundant; and in the dentate gyrus, Clstn1 and Clstn2 were most strongly present (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from single-molecule in situ hybridization shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In the CA3 region, all three calsyntenins were similarly abundant.
source: In the CA1 region, Clstn1 and Clstn3 levels were highest; in the CA3 region, all three calsyntenins were similarly abundant; and in the dentate gyrus, Clstn1 and Clstn2 were most strongly present (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from single-molecule in situ hybridization shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In the dentate gyrus, Clstn1 and Clstn2 were most strongly present.
source: In the CA1 region, Clstn1 and Clstn3 levels were highest; in the CA3 region, all three calsyntenins were similarly abundant; and in the dentate gyrus, Clstn1 and Clstn2 were most strongly present (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from single-molecule in situ hybridization shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Most hippocampal neurons co-express multiple calsyntenin isoforms.
source: These results suggest that most hippocampal neurons co-express multiple calsyntenin isoforms, which may account for the modest phenotypes observed with Clstn1, Clstn2, and Clstn3 KO mice (Kim et al., 2020; Lipina et al., 2016; Pettem et al., 2013; Ster et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the in situ hybridization data showing overlapping expression patterns.

claim: Single-cell RNA transcriptome databases suggest that in the cerebellum, granule cells express primarily Clstn1, while Purkinje cells selectively express Clstn3.
source: We next examined the cerebellum because single-cell RNA transcriptome databases suggested that in the cerebellum, granule cells express primarily Clstn1, while Purkinje cells selectively express Clstn3, suggesting that the expression of calsyntenin isoforms is more segregated in cerebellum than in the hippocampus (Peng et al., 2019; Saunders et al., 2018; Schaum et al., 2018; Tasic et al., 2018; Zeisel et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple single-cell RNA transcriptome databases (Peng et al., 2019; Saunders et al., 2018; Schaum et al., 2018; Tasic et al., 2018; Zeisel et al., 2018).

claim: Purkinje cells in the cerebellum express more than 15-fold higher levels of Clstn3 than Clstn1 or Clstn2.
source: Indeed, quantifications of publicly available single-cell RNAseq data indicated that Purkinje cells in the cerebellum express more than 15-fold higher levels of Clstn3 than Clstn1 or Clstn2, whereas other cell types in the cerebellum primarily express Clstn1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of publicly available single-cell RNAseq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Other cell types in the cerebellum primarily express Clstn1.
source: Indeed, quantifications of publicly available single-cell RNAseq data indicated that Purkinje cells in the cerebellum express more than 15-fold higher levels of Clstn3 than Clstn1 or Clstn2, whereas other cell types in the cerebellum primarily express Clstn1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of publicly available single-cell RNAseq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Single-molecule in situ hybridization of cerebellar sections corroborated that Purkinje cells express almost exclusively Clstn3.
source: Single-molecule in situ hybridization of cerebellar sections corroborated that Purkinje cells express almost exclusively Clstn3, although low amounts of Clstn2 were also detectable, whereas granule cells express Clstn1 (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-molecule in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: Low amounts of Clstn2 were detectable in Purkinje cells.
source: Single-molecule in situ hybridization of cerebellar sections corroborated that Purkinje cells express almost exclusively Clstn3, although low amounts of Clstn2 were also detectable, whereas granule cells express Clstn1 (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-molecule in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: Granule cells express Clstn1.
source: Single-molecule in situ hybridization of cerebellar sections corroborated that Purkinje cells express almost exclusively Clstn3, although low amounts of Clstn2 were also detectable, whereas granule cells express Clstn1 (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-molecule in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: Single-cell qRT-PCR measurements confirmed that Purkinje cells exclusively express high levels of Clstn3 (>20-fold more than Clstn1 or Clstn2).
source: These single-cell qRT-PCR measurements confirmed that Purkinje cells exclusively express high levels of Clstn3 ( > 20-fold more than Clstn1 or Clstn2), whereas other cerebellar neurons do not (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Other cerebellar neurons do not exclusively express high levels of Clstn3.
source: These single-cell qRT-PCR measurements confirmed that Purkinje cells exclusively express high levels of Clstn3 ( > 20-fold more than Clstn1 or Clstn2), whereas other cerebellar neurons do not (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: qRT-PCR measurements on Purkinje cell mRNAs isolated using L7-Cre-dependent ribotag isolation replicated the highly selective expression of Clstn3 in Purkinje cells.
source: Finally, we performed qRT-PCR measurements on Purkinje cell mRNAs isolated using L7-Cre-dependent ribotag isolation (Sanz et al., 2009), and replicated the highly selective expression of Clstn3 in Purkinje cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1E and citation to the ribotag method (Sanz et al., 2009).

claim: The CRISPR-mediated Clstn3 KO decreased Clstn3 mRNA levels by >60%.
source: The CRISPR-mediated Clstn3 KO was highly effective in vivo, decreasing Clstn3 mRNA levels by >60% (Figure 2D and E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), and Clstn3 protein levels by ~80% (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 2D and E, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The CRISPR-mediated Clstn3 KO decreased Clstn3 protein levels by ~80%.
source: The CRISPR-mediated Clstn3 KO was highly effective in vivo, decreasing Clstn3 mRNA levels by >60% (Figure 2D and E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), and Clstn3 protein levels by ~80% (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The AAV-DJ serotype primarily infected Purkinje cells.
source: The AAV-DJ serotype we used primarily infected Purkinje cells as evidenced by the selective presence of the tdTomato signal in Purkinje cells, with very little expression in granule cells and some expression in basket and stellate cells (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data showing tdTomato expression patterns in Figure 2F.

claim: The AAV-DJ serotype showed very little expression in granule cells and some expression in basket and stellate cells.
source: The AAV-DJ serotype we used primarily infected Purkinje cells as evidenced by the selective presence of the tdTomato signal in Purkinje cells, with very little expression in granule cells and some expression in basket and stellate cells (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data showing tdTomato expression patterns in Figure 2F.

claim: Analysis of the Clstn3 CRISPR KO strategy for potential off-target effects demonstrated that at the sites most similar to the Clstn3 target sequence, no mutations were detected.
source: Analysis of the Clstn3 CRISPR KO strategy for potential off-target effects demonstrated that at the sites most similar to the Clstn3 target sequence, no mutations were detected (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-H).
evidence: The claim is supported by genomic sequencing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-H.

claim: Mice with the cerebellar Clstn3 KO exhibited normal open field behavior.
source: Mice with the cerebellar Clstn3 KO exhibited a normal open field behavior, but a striking impairment in motor learning as assayed with the rotarod task (Figure 3A–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3A-E.

claim: Mice with the cerebellar Clstn3 KO exhibited a striking impairment in motor learning as assayed with the rotarod task.
source: Mice with the cerebellar Clstn3 KO exhibited a normal open field behavior, but a striking impairment in motor learning as assayed with the rotarod task (Figure 3A–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3F-G.

claim: The gait of cerebellar Clstn3 KO mice was significantly altered with decreased stride lengths and increased overlap of fore- and hind-paw positions.
source: Moreover, the gait of cerebellar Clstn3 KO mice was significantly altered with decreased stride lengths and increased overlap of fore- and hind-paw positions (Figure 3H–K).
evidence: The claim is supported by gait analysis data shown in Figure 3H-K.

claim: The cerebellar Clstn3 KO mice displayed normal beam walk abilities and normal social behaviors.
source: However, the cerebellar Clstn3 KO mice displayed normal beam walk abilities and normal social behaviors, suggesting that the observed motor impairments are selective (Figure 3L–R).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3L-R.

claim: The motor coordination deficit in Clstn3 CRISPR KO mice is consistent with phenotypes observed in constitutive Clstn3 KO mice.
source: The motor coordination deficit in Clstn3 CRISPR KO mice is consistent with phenotypes observed in constitutive Clstn3 KO mice (https://www.mousephenotype.org) (Dickinson et al., 2016), suggesting that our CRISPR KO approach is reliable and specific.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to published data from constitutive KO mice (Dickinson et al., 2016).

claim: The CRISPR KO of Clstn3 in the cerebellum robustly reduced the inhibitory synapse density in the molecular layer, Purkinje-cell layer, and granule-cell layer of the cerebellar cortex.
source: The CRISPR KO of Clstn3 in the cerebellum robustly reduced the inhibitory synapse density in the molecular layer, Purkinje-cell layer, and granule-cell layer of the cerebellar cortex as measured both with the pre- and the postsynaptic marker.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The most extensive decrease (~60–70%) in inhibitory synapse density was observed in the deep molecular layer.
source: The most extensive decrease (~60–70%) was observed in the deep molecular layer (Figure 4B and F), where we also detected a significant reduction (~25%) in the size of vGAT-positive puncta, which correspond to the presynaptic vesicle clusters of inhibitory synapses (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4B and F.

claim: A significant reduction (~25%) in the size of vGAT-positive puncta was detected in the deep molecular layer.
source: The most extensive decrease (~60–70%) was observed in the deep molecular layer (Figure 4B and F), where we also detected a significant reduction (~25%) in the size of vGAT-positive puncta, which correspond to the presynaptic vesicle clusters of inhibitory synapses (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: vGAT- and GABA-Aα1 receptor-positive synapses in Purkinje cell and granule cell layers exhibited a robust decrease (~20% reduction).
source: vGAT- and GABA-Aα1 receptor-positive synapses in Purkinje cell and granule cell layers were less affected, but still exhibited a robust decrease (~20% reduction; Figure 4D and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4D and H.

claim: The Clstn3 KO produced a large decrease in mIPSC frequency (~60%).
source: The Clstn3 KO produced a large decrease in mIPSC frequency (~60%), without changing the mIPSC amplitude (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: The Clstn3 KO did not change the mIPSC amplitude.
source: The Clstn3 KO produced a large decrease in mIPSC frequency (~60%), without changing the mIPSC amplitude (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: The Clstn3 KO increased the rise but not decay times of mIPSCs.
source: Moreover, the Clstn3 KO increased the rise but not decay times of mIPSCs (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The Clstn3 deletion did not produce major changes in Purkinje cell capacitance and input resistance.
source: Measurements of the Purkinje cell capacitance and input resistance showed that the Clstn3 deletion did not produce major changes, demonstrating that it did not globally alter Purkinje cell properties (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Both classes of mIPSCs (>60 pA and <60 pA) exhibited similar impairments in frequency.
source: Importantly, both classes of mIPSCs exhibited similar impairments in frequency, although the changes were slightly more pronounced for larger mIPSCs (Figure 5F–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5F-H.

claim: The changes in mIPSC frequency were slightly more pronounced for larger mIPSCs.
source: Importantly, both classes of mIPSCs exhibited similar impairments in frequency, although the changes were slightly more pronounced for larger mIPSCs (Figure 5F–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5F-H.

claim: The Clstn3 KO caused a significant decrease (~40%) in IPSC amplitudes.
source: These measurements revealed a significant decrease (~40%) in IPSC amplitudes.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6.

claim: No major changes in the coefficient of variation, paired-pulse ratio, or kinetics of evoked IPSCs were detected.
source: However, we detected no major changes in the coefficient of variation, paired-pulse ratio, or kinetics of evoked IPSCs, suggesting that the release probability is normal (Figure 6B–F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6B-F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Parallel-fiber synapses use the vesicular glutamate transporter vGluT1.
source: Parallel-fiber synapses use the vesicular glutamate transporter vGluT1, whereas climbing-fiber synapses use the vesicular glutamate transporter vGluT2 (Hioki et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hioki et al., 2003 and represents established knowledge.

claim: Climbing-fiber synapses use the vesicular glutamate transporter vGluT2.
source: Parallel-fiber synapses use the vesicular glutamate transporter vGluT1, whereas climbing-fiber synapses use the vesicular glutamate transporter vGluT2 (Hioki et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hioki et al., 2003 and represents established knowledge.

claim: Parallel-fiber synapses are surrounded by astrocytic processes formed by Bergmann glia, creating a tripartite synapse in which the glial processes contain high levels of GluA1.
source: Moreover, parallel-fiber synapses are surrounded by astrocytic processes formed by Bergmann glia, creating a tripartite synapse in which the glial processes contain high levels of GluA1 (Baude et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Baude et al., 1994 and represents established knowledge.

claim: The cerebellar Clstn3 deletion caused a robust increase (>25%) in the vGluT1 staining intensity of both the superficial and the deep molecular layers of the cerebellar cortex.
source: The cerebellar Clstn3 deletion caused a robust increase ( > 25%) in the vGluT1 staining intensity of both the superficial and the deep molecular layers of the cerebellar cortex (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The cerebellar Clstn3 KO induced an even more striking increase (~80%) in GluA2 staining in Purkinje cells.
source: The cerebellar Clstn3 KO induced an even more striking increase (~80%) in GluA2 staining in Purkinje cells than that observed for vGluT1 staining (Figure 7C and D), demonstrating that immunohistochemistry for both pre- and postsynaptic parallel-fiber synapses reveal an increase in parallel-fiber synapses induced by the cerebellar Clstn3 KO.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: The cerebellar Clstn3 KO induced a significant enhancement (~25%) in synaptic GluA1 staining intensity.
source: Again, the cerebellar Clstn3 KO induced a significant enhancement (~25%) in synaptic GluA1 staining intensity (Figure 7F), consistent with the increase in vGluT1 and GluA2 staining intensity.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The number and size of synaptic puncta identified with vGluT2 antibodies were not altered by the Clstn3 KO.
source: The number and size of synaptic puncta identified with vGluT2 antibodies were not altered by the Clstn3 KO, although there was a slight trend towards a decrease in climbing-fiber synapse density (Figure 7H, I).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7H and I.

claim: There was a slight trend towards a decrease in climbing-fiber synapse density.
source: The number and size of synaptic puncta identified with vGluT2 antibodies were not altered by the Clstn3 KO, although there was a slight trend towards a decrease in climbing-fiber synapse density (Figure 7H, I).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7H and I.

claim: The dendritic spine density of Purkinje cells is a useful, but imperfect, proxy of parallel-fiber synapses because in a normal brain, all spines contain parallel-fiber synapses and all parallel-fiber synapses are on spines.
source: The dendritic spine density of Purkinje cells is a useful, but imperfect, proxy of parallel-fiber synapses because in a normal brain, all spines contain parallel-fiber synapses and all parallel-fiber synapses are on spines (Sotelo, 1975).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Sotelo, 1975 and represents established knowledge.

claim: Some mutations, such as the Cbln1 deletion, cause a partial loss of parallel-fiber synapses and induce the appearance of 'naked' spines.
source: However, some mutations, such as the Cbln1 deletion (Yuzaki and Aricescu, 2017), cause a partial loss of parallel-fiber synapses and induce the appearance of 'naked' spines.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Yuzaki and Aricescu, 2017.

claim: Reconstructions revealed a trend toward an increased dendrite length in Clstn3-deficient Purkinje cells without a significant change in dendritic architecture.
source: These reconstructions revealed a trend toward an increased dendrite length in Clstn3-deficient Purkinje cells without a significant change in dendritic architecture, demonstrating that the Clstn3 KO does not impair the overall structure of Purkinje cells (Figure 8B).
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological reconstruction data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Quantification of dendritic spines uncovered in Clstn3-deficient Purkinje cells a robust increase (~30%) in the density of spines in the superficial area of the cerebellar cortex.
source: Quantification of dendritic spines uncovered in Clstn3-deficient Purkinje cells a robust increase (~30%) in the density of spines in the superficial area of the cerebellar cortex, and a trend toward an increase in the deep area of the cerebellar cortex (Figure 8C–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological data shown in Figure 8C-F.

claim: There was a trend toward an increase in spine density in the deep area of the cerebellar cortex.
source: Quantification of dendritic spines uncovered in Clstn3-deficient Purkinje cells a robust increase (~30%) in the density of spines in the superficial area of the cerebellar cortex, and a trend toward an increase in the deep area of the cerebellar cortex (Figure 8C–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological data shown in Figure 8C-F.

claim: The increase in spine density was particularly pronounced for thin spines.
source: The increase in spine density was particularly pronounced for thin spines (Figure 8G; Figure 8—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological data shown in Figure 8G and Figure 8—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: An increase in mEPSC amplitudes (~25%) and frequency (~15%) was observed in Clstn3 KO neurons.
source: We observed an increase in mEPSC amplitudes (~25%) and frequency (~15%) in Clstn3 KO neurons, without a notable change in mEPSC kinetics (Figure 9A-D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 9A-D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: No notable change in mEPSC kinetics was observed in Clstn3 KO neurons.
source: We observed an increase in mEPSC amplitudes (~25%) and frequency (~15%) in Clstn3 KO neurons, without a notable change in mEPSC kinetics (Figure 9A-D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 9A-D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The Clstn3 KO robustly enhanced parallel-fiber synaptic responses (~60% increase).
source: Consistent with the morphological and mEPSC data, the Clstn3 KO robustly enhanced parallel-fiber synaptic responses (~60% increase) (Figure 10B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 10B-D.

claim: The increased strength of parallel-fiber synaptic transmission was not due to a change in release probability.
source: The increased strength of parallel-fiber synaptic transmission was not due to a change in release probability because neither the coefficient of variation nor the paired-pulse ratios of parallel-fiber EPSCs were altered (Figure 10E–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 10E-G.

claim: The amplitude, coefficient of variation, paired-pulse ratio, and kinetics of climbing-fiber EPSCs in control and Clstn3 KO Purkinje cells were indistinguishable.
source: Specifically, the amplitude, paired-pulse ratio, and kinetics of climbing-fiber EPSCs in control and Clstn3 KO Purkinje cells were indistinguishable (Figure 10H-L, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 10H-L and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The sparse deletion of Clstn3 only suppressed Clstn3 levels but not Clstn1 or Clstn2 levels in Purkinje cells.
source: The sparse deletion of Clstn3 only suppressed Clstn3 levels but not Clstn1 or Clstn2 levels in Purkinje cells, and only suppressed Clstn3 levels in Purkinje cells but not in surrounding granule or basket cells (Figure 11—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 11—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The sparse deletion of Clstn3 only suppressed Clstn3 levels in Purkinje cells but not in surrounding granule or basket cells.
source: The sparse deletion of Clstn3 only suppressed Clstn3 levels but not Clstn1 or Clstn2 levels in Purkinje cells, and only suppressed Clstn3 levels in Purkinje cells but not in surrounding granule or basket cells (Figure 11—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 11—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The sparse Clstn3 deletion suppressed the strength of inhibitory synapses in Purkinje cells similar to the Clstn3 deletion in the entire cerebellar cortex (~60% decrease).
source: Strikingly, the sparse Clstn3 deletion suppressed the strength of inhibitory synapses in Purkinje cells similar to the Clstn3 deletion in the entire cerebellar cortex (~60% decrease; Figure 11C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 11C-E.

claim: The sparse Clstn3 deletion increased the strength of parallel-fiber synapses (~100% increase).
source: At the same time and in the same type of neurons, the sparse Clstn3 deletion increased the strength of parallel-fiber synapses (~100% increase; Figure 11F–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 11F-H.

claim: Both the decrease in inhibitory synaptic strength and the increase in excitatory parallel-fiber synapse strength were not associated with significant alterations in the coefficient of variation or paired-pulse ratio of synaptic responses.
source: Both the decrease in inhibitory synaptic strength and the increase in excitatory parallel-fiber synapse strength were not associated with significant alterations in the coefficient of variation or paired-pulse ratio of synaptic responses (Figure 11D, E, I and J), which is consistent with the changes in synapse numbers observed morphologically after pan-cerebellar Clstn3 deletions (Figures 4, 7 and 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 11D, E, I and J.

claim: Clstn3 acts as a postsynaptic adhesion molecule in Purkinje cells that is selectively essential for regulating synapse numbers.
source: Our data establish that Clstn3 acts as a postsynaptic adhesion molecule in Purkinje cells that is selectively essential for regulating synapse numbers, confirming an essential function for Clstn3 as a postsynaptic adhesion molecule.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The deletion of Clstn3 causes a decrease in inhibitory basket- and stellate-cell synapses on Purkinje cells, but an increase in excitatory parallel-fiber synapses.
source: Specifically, our results demonstrate that the deletion of Clstn3 causes a decrease in inhibitory basket- and stellate-cell synapses on Purkinje cells, but an increase in excitatory parallel-fiber synapses (Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Clstn3 acts as a regulator of the balance of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic inputs on Purkinje cells.
source: Thus, Clstn3 does not function simply as a synaptogenic adhesion molecule, but acts as a regulator of the balance of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic inputs on Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: At present, only two families of adhesion-GPCRs, latrophilins and BAIs, are known to have a major impact on synapse numbers when tested using rigorous genetic approaches.
source: At present, only two families of adhesion-GPCRs, latrophilins and BAIs, are known to have a major impact on synapse numbers when tested using rigorous genetic approaches (Anderson et al., 2017; Bolliger et al., 2011, Kakegawa et al., 2015; Sando et al., 2019; Sando and Südhof, 2021; Sigoillot et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: The majority of SAMs that have been studied, most prominently neurexins and LAR-type receptor phosphotyrosine phosphatases, appear to be dispensable for establishing synaptic connections.
source: In contrast, the majority of SAMs that have been studied, most prominently neurexins and LAR-type receptor phosphotyrosine phosphatases, appear to be dispensable for establishing synaptic connections. Instead, these SAMs are essential for conferring onto existing synapses specific properties that differ between various types of synapses in a neural circuit (Chen et al., 2017; Emperador-Melero et al., 2021; Fukai and Yoshida, 2021, Missler et al., 2003; Sclip and Südhof, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: Acute CRISPR-mediated deletion of calsyntenin-3 in mouse cerebellum in vivo causes a large decrease in inhibitory synapse.
source: Here, we show that, surprisingly, acute CRISPR-mediated deletion of calsyntenin-3 in mouse cerebellum in vivo causes a large decrease in inhibitory synapse, but a robust increase in excitatory parallel-fiber synapses in Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Acute CRISPR-mediated deletion of calsyntenin-3 in mouse cerebellum in vivo causes a robust increase in excitatory parallel-fiber synapses in Purkinje cells.
source: Here, we show that, surprisingly, acute CRISPR-mediated deletion of calsyntenin-3 in mouse cerebellum in vivo causes a large decrease in inhibitory synapse, but a robust increase in excitatory parallel-fiber synapses in Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Inhibitory synaptic transmission was suppressed by the calsyntenin-3 deletion.
source: As a result, inhibitory synaptic transmission was suppressed, whereas parallel-fiber synaptic transmission was enhanced in Purkinje cells by the calsyntenin-3 deletion.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings supported by electrophysiology data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Parallel-fiber synaptic transmission was enhanced in Purkinje cells by the calsyntenin-3 deletion.
source: As a result, inhibitory synaptic transmission was suppressed, whereas parallel-fiber synaptic transmission was enhanced in Purkinje cells by the calsyntenin-3 deletion.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings supported by electrophysiology data throughout the manuscript.

claim: No changes in the dendritic architecture of Purkinje cells were detected after calsyntenin-3 deletion.
source: No changes in the dendritic architecture of Purkinje cells or in climbing-fiber synapses were detected.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings supported by morphological data in Figure 8.

claim: No changes in climbing-fiber synapses were detected after calsyntenin-3 deletion.
source: No changes in the dendritic architecture of Purkinje cells or in climbing-fiber synapses were detected.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings supported by immunohistochemistry and electrophysiology data in Figures 7 and 10.

claim: Sparse selective deletion of calsyntenin-3 only in Purkinje cells recapitulated the synaptic phenotype.
source: Sparse selective deletion of calsyntenin-3 only in Purkinje cells recapitulated the synaptic phenotype, indicating that calsyntenin-3 acts by a cell-autonomous postsynaptic mechanism in cerebellum.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings supported by data in Figure 11.

claim: Calsyntenin-3 acts by a cell-autonomous postsynaptic mechanism in cerebellum.
source: Sparse selective deletion of calsyntenin-3 only in Purkinje cells recapitulated the synaptic phenotype, indicating that calsyntenin-3 acts by a cell-autonomous postsynaptic mechanism in cerebellum.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the sparse deletion experiments showing that Purkinje cell-specific deletion is sufficient to produce the phenotype.

claim: By inhibiting formation of excitatory parallel-fiber synapses and promoting formation of inhibitory synapses in the same neuron, calsyntenin-3 functions as a postsynaptic adhesion molecule that regulates the excitatory/inhibitory balance in Purkinje cells.
source: Thus, by inhibiting formation of excitatory parallel-fiber synapses and promoting formation of inhibitory synapses in the same neuron, calsyntenin-3 functions as a postsynaptic adhesion molecule that regulates the excitatory/inhibitory balance in Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from all the experimental data presented in the manuscript.
